items.stem: A food delivery app's developer reads every request that reaches the app's own server during a card payment. Will the card number appear in them?

options.text: No. The browser sends the card to the gateway, and the app's server gets only a token
options.feedback: Because the card number never enters the app's systems, they stay out of PCI DSS scope.

options.text: Yes, because the card goes from the browser to the app's server and then to the gateway
options.feedback: If that were the design, the app's server would fall under PCI DSS. Gateways exist so the card skips the app's server.

options.text: Yes, but only when the payment fails and the app has to retry the charge
options.feedback: The card number does not reach the app's server at all, whether the payment succeeds or fails.

items.stem: Your server asks the gateway to charge a user's e-wallet, and the gateway replies with the status `pending`. What should the app do?

options.text: Show the order as awaiting payment, and mark it paid when the webhook arrives
options.feedback: Wallet payments can take minutes or hours. The webhook is the gateway's final confirmation.

options.text: Mark the order paid right away, because the gateway accepted the request
options.feedback: Accepting the request means the payment started. Money has not moved yet, and the payment may still fail.

options.text: Show an error to the user, because pending means the payment failed
options.feedback: Pending means the result is not known yet. It does not mean failure.

items.stem: A user presses Pay three times on a stalled checkout. The app sends no idempotency key. How many charges does the user pay?

options.text: Three, because each POST creates a separate charge
options.feedback: POST is not idempotent, and each request was valid. Nothing tells the gateway the three requests belong together.

options.text: One, because the server notices the duplicates
options.feedback: The server sees three valid requests with no sign that they are repeats. It cannot tell them apart from three real purchases.

options.text: One, because the gateway rejects repeated amounts
options.feedback: A user can legitimately pay the same amount twice, so gateways cannot reject on amount alone. They need a key.

items.try: In the step "A double charge", leave the key off, press Pay three times and read the total. Then turn the key on and try again.

items.stem: The gateway takes 800 ms to answer. Your server waits for it inside each request, and you have 4 workers. About how many requests per second can the server finish?

options.text: About 4.8, because each request holds a worker for 0.84 seconds
options.feedback: Four workers divided by 0.84 seconds is about 4.8 requests per second. Moving the gateway call to a background queue raises this to about 100.

options.text: About 100, because your own code takes only 40 ms per request
options.feedback: That is the figure only if the gateway call happens outside the request. While a worker waits for the gateway, it cannot serve anyone else.

options.text: There is no limit, because a waiting worker does not use the server
options.feedback: A waiting worker is still occupied. With 4 workers, 4 slow requests use all of them.
